questions.question: A table `order_items(order_id, product_id, product_name, qty)` has the composite primary key `(order_id, product_id)`. `product_name` depends only on `product_id`. What normal form does this violate?
options: 1NF, because product_name is not atomic
2NF, because product_name is a Partial Dependency on only part of the composite key
3NF, because product_name is a Transitive Dependency
BCNF, because product_id is not a superkey
questions.explanation: 2NF requires that every non-key attribute depend on the entire primary key, not just part of it. Here, product_name depends only on product_id (part of the composite key), not on the full (order_id, product_id) pair — this is the textbook definition of a Partial Dependency. The fix is to move product_name into its own products table keyed by product_id alone, leaving order_items to store only the relationship and quantity.

questions.question: Why does SQL forbid storing a list like `['red', 'blue']` directly in a single column under 1NF?
options: Because lists take up more disk space than single values
Because non-atomic values make filtering, indexing, and aggregating by individual list members unreliable, typically forcing slow pattern-matching like LIKE
Because Postgres has no array data type
Because 1NF only applies to numeric columns
questions.explanation: 1NF requires every column value to be atomic (a single, indivisible value) so the relational model's core operations -- equality filtering, grouping, indexing -- work correctly. A packed list like 'red,blue' can only be searched with a fragile LIKE '%blue%' pattern, which is both slow (no useful index) and can produce false positives (matching 'skyblue'). Splitting into a child table with one row per list element restores clean WHERE/GROUP BY/JOIN semantics.

questions.question: A table `enrollments(student_id, course_id, instructor)` has primary key `(student_id, course_id)`. Each course has exactly one instructor, so `course_id -> instructor`. Why does this fail BCNF even though it may pass 3NF?
options: Because instructor is not an atomic value
Because course_id, the determinant of the dependency course_id -> instructor, is not by itself a candidate key (superkey) of the table
Because student_id and course_id should never be combined into one key
Because BCNF requires every table to have exactly one column
questions.explanation: BCNF's rule is stricter than 3NF: for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey -- capable of determining every column in the table on its own. Here course_id determines instructor, but course_id alone cannot determine student_id, so course_id is not a superkey of this table. This is exactly the gap BCNF closes that 3NF's transitive-dependency check (which only examines non-key-to-non-key dependencies) can miss. The fix is decomposing into courses(course_id, instructor) and enrollments(student_id, course_id).

questions.question: Why is a surrogate key (auto-increment ID or UUID) generally preferred over a natural key (like email) as a table's PRIMARY KEY?
options: Surrogate keys are always shorter in storage
Surrogate keys never change, so foreign keys referencing them never need to cascade-update when real-world attributes change
Natural keys cannot be made UNIQUE
Surrogate keys make JOINs run faster on every database engine, with no exceptions
questions.explanation: A surrogate key has no business meaning, so nothing in the outside world ever forces it to change -- it is purely an internal handle. A natural key like email can change (marriage, rebranding, typo correction), and if every foreign key referencing that user is built on the email value itself, a single email change would need to cascade through every child table. The standard pattern is to use a surrogate key as the PK for stability while still enforcing the natural key's uniqueness with a UNIQUE constraint.

questions.question: Why do data warehouses (OLAP) deliberately denormalize into a Star Schema instead of keeping everything in 3NF?
options: Because analysts cannot write JOIN syntax
Because aggregation queries over millions of rows become slower as join depth increases, and flattening dimension hierarchies into the fact table reduces the number of joins needed
Because 3NF tables cannot store numeric data
Because Star Schemas use less disk space than 3NF tables
questions.explanation: OLAP workloads run large aggregations (SUM/GROUP BY) across huge fact tables, and every additional join in the query plan adds I/O and CPU cost that multiplies at scale. By denormalizing dimension hierarchies (e.g., product -> subcategory -> category) into a single category_name column on the fact table or a flat dimension table, a 'revenue by category' query touches far fewer tables. The anomaly risk this reintroduces is acceptable because warehouse data is refreshed via controlled ETL/ELT pipelines from upstream 3NF source-of-truth systems, not live ad hoc writes.

questions.question: A `sales.product_id` foreign key is defined `ON DELETE CASCADE`. What happens when someone deletes a row from `products`, and why is this often the wrong choice for a sales/products relationship?
options: The delete is blocked with an error; CASCADE never allows deletion
All matching sales rows for that product are automatically deleted too, silently destroying historical revenue records
The product_id column in sales is set to NULL, preserving the sales rows
Nothing happens until VACUUM runs
questions.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE means deleting the parent row automatically deletes every child row that references it. For a products-to-sales relationship, this is usually wrong: deleting a discontinued product would silently erase the historical sales records tied to it, understating revenue in any report run afterward. ON DELETE RESTRICT is the safer choice here -- it blocks the deletion outright unless the dependent sales rows are explicitly archived or reassigned first, forcing a deliberate decision instead of an accidental data loss.

questions.question: When is ON DELETE SET NULL the correct referential integrity strategy?
options: Whenever a table has more than one foreign key
When the child row should be preserved for historical/compliance reasons but no longer needs to be tied to a deleted parent -- e.g., orders surviving a GDPR-driven customer erasure
When the parent table is append-only
It is never correct in production systems
questions.explanation: ON DELETE SET NULL keeps the child row but clears the foreign key column when the parent is deleted -- ideal when the child record has independent value (like financial/tax history) but the link to the now-erased parent must be severed. The canonical example is a GDPR/soft-delete scenario: erasing a customer's PII should not erase their order history, so orders.customer_id becomes NULL while the order itself, and its tax-relevant totals, remain intact for compliance reporting.

questions.question: Per the 'Over-Normalization' pitfall, when should you NOT split a column like Address into Street_Number, Street_Name, Suffix, and Apartment?
options: Never split addresses under any circumstance
When no query in the system ever needs to filter, aggregate, or join on the individual address components -- a single text column (or JSONB) is the correct, senior-level choice
Only when the address is for a residential customer rather than a business
Always split it, because more normalization is always better design
questions.explanation: Normalization is a tool for eliminating redundancy and preventing anomalies, not an aesthetic end in itself. If nothing in the application ever runs WHERE street_suffix = 'Ave' or aggregates by apartment number, decomposing the address into five columns only adds insertion complexity and more places for a NULL or typo to creep in, with zero query benefit. The senior-level judgment call is to normalize exactly what you need to filter, aggregate, or constrain via foreign key, and leave the rest as a single opaque field.
